lesson.title: The Great Commoner and the Cross of Gold
lesson.summary: In 1896, a thirty six year old congressman from Nebraska electrified the Democratic National Convention with a defense of free silver and rural America, becoming the youngest major party presidential nominee in United States history.
lesson.body:
William Jennings Bryan was born in Salem, Illinois, in 1860 and later settled in Nebraska, where he practiced law and won election to the United States House of Representatives in 1890 at the age of thirty. He quickly built a reputation as one of the most powerful public speakers of his generation, and his politics closely tracked the grievances of the Populist movement covered in the previous chapter, even though Bryan ran as a Democrat rather than a Populist.

By 1896, the Democratic Party was bitterly split between a pro gold standard, pro business wing associated with outgoing President Grover Cleveland, and an agrarian wing demanding the free coinage of silver. At the party's national convention in Chicago that July, Bryan, still not a national figure, rose during the platform debate to defend free silver and to speak for farmers and workers against what he portrayed as the indifference of eastern financial interests. He closed with a line that instantly became famous: "You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns, you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." The convention hall erupted, and the next day delegates nominated Bryan for president, making him, at thirty six, the youngest major party nominee in American history.

The Populist Party, meeting separately that same summer, chose to endorse Bryan rather than field its own candidate, a fusion strategy that folded much of the Populist coalition into the Democratic campaign. Fusion strengthened Bryan in the West and South, but it also blurred the Populists' distinct identity and hastened the party's decline as an independent political force.

In the general election, Bryan campaigned relentlessly, traveling thousands of miles by train and delivering hundreds of speeches directly to voters, an unusual strategy for the time. His Republican opponent, William McKinley, ran a more traditional "front porch" campaign from his home in Ohio, backed by a much larger campaign fund organized by Mark Hanna. McKinley won, helped by industrial workers and business interests who feared that free silver's inflation would erode real wages and savings.

Bryan remained a major figure in American politics for decades. He ran for president again in 1900 and 1908, losing both times, and later served as Secretary of State under President Woodrow Wilson from 1913 to 1915, resigning in protest over the administration's handling of neutrality during World War One. In his later years he became a leading opponent of teaching evolution in public schools and served as a prosecuting attorney in the 1925 Scopes trial in Dayton, Tennessee, dying only days after the trial concluded.
